purpose: Consolidated A/B for the prose ui-* family (13 skills + visual-hierarchy, roughly 2,800 lines) with visual-hierarchy evaluated in the same run but flagged as a separate decision. ui-color and ui-spacing are already converted to objective + runnable check and stay installed in all arms; this run isolates whether the remaining ui prose changes answer quality beyond the base model. Routing/effect-boundary cases stay in high_use_cases.json; this file is quality cases only and is deliberately not parsed by validate_registry.py.

arms.A_control: Active registry WITH the prose ui-* family installed (ui-actions, ui-content, ui-data-viz, ui-depth, ui-email, ui-feedback, ui-forms, ui-icons, ui-layouts, ui-onboarding, ui-patterns, ui-responsive, ui-typography, visual-hierarchy, plus the ui-expert routing table) — the registry as of 2026-08-15 including the two converted checkers.
arms.B_bare: Same registry WITH the prose ui-* family removed to archive/ui-evicted/. Only the converted checkers (ui-color, ui-spacing) and their checks remain; no ui-expert router.
arms.C_substitute: Arm B plus the substitution context in docs/ui-substitute-note.md: axe-core + Playwright screenshot diffs as the ground-truth checks and the kept convert checks. Runs only where mean(A) - mean(B) > 0.15 (recovery test).

protocol: Run each case 3x per arm in fresh context. Score each answer 0-1: (fraction of must_include anchors satisfied) minus 0.34 for each must_avoid anchor present, floored at 0. Record raw answers before scores in a dated results/ file. A rubric-judge model may score, but must see only prompt + answer + anchors, never the arm label. Exclude degenerate reps (returned preamble only) and note them in the report.
gate: The family is safe to EVICT when mean(B) >= mean(A) - 0.10 AND arm B commits no must_exclude violation on any case where arm A commits none. A case where A beats B by >0.25 and C does NOT recover it flags that specific sub-skill as a CONVERT candidate (keep a check, not the prose), not a blanket keep. Because these are UX judgments, tag each case `canonical` (well-known trap the model has internalized) or `openjudgment` (genuine trade-off where taste/context matters); a tied openjudgment case is stronger evidence than a tied canonical one — say which in the report.

cases.prompt: Our new invoices screen has no rows yet. What should we show instead of a blank table? Also, what should the empty-state button label be?
must_include: an empty state that explains the current state and offers the primary next action
copy that names the object/action without duplicating the page heading
a concrete primary action the user can take to get value
must_exclude: showing only a bare 'No invoices' message with no action
vague marketing copy that does not name the action

cases.prompt: Every row in our projects table has 6 actions (edit, duplicate, share, archive, export, delete). All 6 as icon buttons feels noisy and wide. How should I present row-level actions?
must_include: only the 1-2 primary actions stay visible inline; the rest go in an overflow (kebab/ellipsis) menu
destructive actions sit last in the overflow, not inline first
actions the user takes often stay visible; rare ones move to the menu
must_exclude: recommending every action as a visible icon button
putting delete as the first inline action

cases.prompt: Our dashboard shows total users over 12 months in a card, plus a second card with this month's total. I am choosing between a full line chart and a big number with a small trend indicator for the second card. Which and why?
must_include: the single current-month total is a big number with a tiny trend indicator, not a full chart
the 12-month series earns a line chart because the shape over time matters
match chart to data density; one number does not need an axis
must_exclude: recommending a pie or donut for the current-month total
same chart treatment for both cards regardless of data

cases.prompt: Cards, a modal, and a dropdown on one page all use the same large shadow and read as one blob. How do I differentiate elevation so depth reads without clutter?
must_include: a limited elevation scale (resting / raised / overlay) mapped to component types
differentiate with surface tone, borders, and layering, not shadow size alone
modal + backdrop sit above the page layer; cards stay at rest
must_exclude: advising one shared shadow value for consistency
implying all floating UI needs the same drop shadow

cases.prompt: My order-confirmation email renders fine in Gmail but breaks in Outlook: grid columns collapse and image spacing multiplies. What is the general approach to authoring cross-client email?
must_include: target the worst client (Outlook): table-based layout and inline styles, not grid/flexbox
degrade gracefully: keep content readable when a style is dropped
test in real clients (Litmus or mail clients), not just a browser
must_exclude: recommending flexbox/grid layout as safe across clients
claiming it works because GMail renders it

cases.prompt: A user submits a form and the server times out. Should I show a toast? The app is also half-down, so a persistent system banner exists. How do I choose between inline error, toast, and banner here?
must_include: field validation/errors live inline next to the field
the transient post-submit failure is a toast (short-lived, dismissible, retry offered)
a durable outage is a banner/modal with an explicit action, not a toast
must_exclude: using a toast for a repeated inline field error
using a modal for a transient failure that a toast handles

cases.prompt: A settings nav has 3 sections. One section holds 30 toggles and sliders; the other two have 5 fields each. Same page or tabs? And is toggles-everywhere even right?
must_include: 30 controls on one page is too much; group by purpose or split into tabs/sections
toggles suit binary, frequently-changed choices; mutual-exclusive options should be radio/select
a destructive or rarely-changed setting deserves a distinct control (button/confirm), not a silent toggle
must_exclude: using a toggle for mutually exclusive options
a modal for any form with more than a handful of fields

cases.prompt: We want a delete row with only a trash icon and a profile icon button, no text. Is icon-only acceptable? What exactly is required for it?
must_include: an icon-only button needs an accessible name (aria-label/title), not a tooltip-only label
icons must be recognizable in context; ambiguous actions should be text-labeled or paired
hover-dependent meaning is a failure for keyboard and touch users
must_exclude: a tooltip as the only accessible name
using the identical icon for two distinct actions

cases.prompt: We have a settings page with 3 sections: account profile (5 fields), notifications (2 toggles), and permissions (2 selects). It looks thin and empty. Should I reorganize as cards, tabs, or a dashboard layout?
must_include: small-scope settings belong as simple grouped sections or tabs on one page, not a dashboard
do not invent cards, stat tiles, or side metrics to fill whitespace
a dashboard grid is for operational data, not for a small settings surface
must_exclude: adding unrelated analytics cards 'so it does not look empty'
a full-screen landing-page hero for a settings page

cases.prompt: New users land on an empty project board. We spent a while reasoning about whether to show a checklist tour, a product-tour tooltip, or a blank-slate card. What is the better onboarding approach and when?
must_include: orchestrate for value quickly: the empty state itself is the onboarding moment
a scripted multi-step tour is for complex flows; a one-line action is enough for a simple board
avoid coercing power users through a fixed tour; keep the path skippable and reversible
must_exclude: a full-screen checklist modal before any value is visible
forcing a 6-step tooltip tour on first visit

cases.prompt: We display 40 deployments per environment. Customers need to scan by column (name, status, age, commit). Is a table, a card list, or a tile grid the right pattern here?
must_include: data with repeatable columns and a scan-by-column need is a table
cards/lists serve heterogeneous or media-heavy content and lower density
with 40 rows, offer filtering/search even if an expert table is fine
must_exclude: converting a scan-by-column list into a big-card list that breaks alignment
removing pagination/filter evidence because table is 'the pattern'

cases.prompt: Our desktop table is 9 columns wide. Which responsive pattern is the right one for narrow phones: horizontal scroll, collapse to cards, hide columns, or a separate view?
must_include: choose a pattern by task: collapse to stacked cards for scannable cards, hide the least-needed columns for comparison scanning, dedicated view for edit-heavy tables
rule: a reorganized stacked layout still keeps the primary columns visible
never silently cut business-critical columns on small screens without a check
must_exclude: hiding entire columns that are the primary action on desktop
advising one universal responsive pattern for all tables

cases.prompt: We need a type scale for a marketing + app dashboard. We have 9 font sizes in use across screens. How do we build a sane scale from this?
must_include: a modular base scale (e.g. 1.25 ratio) yields a small set; bind 3-4 hierarchical roles (title, heading, body, caption) rather than every size
body text weight and size first, then headings sized relative to body
map existing 9 sizes into roles; drop unused sizes, keep < so the scale stays tight
must_exclude: prescribing 9 unrelated sizes as solids
using a chart/display font for body copy

cases.prompt: A settings page has a big hero title, a prominent install banner, small form labels, and every button equally styled. Users cannot see what to do first. How do I fix the hierarchy without adding color or larger whitespace?
must_include: rank: decide the controlling task, restructure title + action + content to serve it
reduce prominence of the co-equal banner (less visual weight) so one thing dominates
emphasis via grouping, spacing, type weight, not brightness and color alone
must_exclude: making everything bigger and stronger
adding a strong color to every primary button
